title: Raised beds
teaches: Choosing a raised bed's height, filling it with a mix that holds its level and drains into the ground below, and keeping it watered and fed

blocks.text: A raised bed is a block of soil lifted above the surrounding ground and held in by a frame of timber, stone, brick, or metal. Lifting the soil changes how it behaves in several ways at once. Rain drains out of a raised bed faster than out of the ground around it, so a bed built over heavy clay becomes workable days sooner after wet weather. The soil also warms earlier in spring, partly because sun and air reach its sides as well as its top and partly because drier soil takes less heat to warm,[^warming] which lets gardeners in cool climates sow a week or two sooner. Because the frame marks clearly where the growing area ends, nobody walks on the soil, and the crumb structure described in Lesson 6 survives from one year to the next.

The same features bring costs. A raised bed dries out faster in summer and cools faster in autumn, and it has to be filled with soil brought from somewhere else, which is usually the largest expense of building one. Sides 20 to 30 cm high are enough for most vegetables, provided the ground beneath the bed is loosened so that roots can grow on down into it. Taller beds of 45 cm or more make sense over paving, waterlogged ground, or contaminated soil, or for a gardener who finds kneeling and bending difficult and wants to work sitting on the edge of the frame.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Raised beds drain faster, warm earlier in spring, and keep feet off the soil, but they dry out faster in summer and cost money to fill.
A bed 20 to 30 cm deep suits most vegetables over loosened ground, while beds of 45 cm or more suit paving, waterlogged or contaminated ground, and gardeners who prefer to sit while they work.

blocks.text: To work out how much fill a bed needs, multiply its length, width, and depth in metres to get its volume in cubic metres, and multiply that by 1000 for litres. A bed 2.4 m long, 1.2 m wide, and 30 cm deep holds about 0.86 cubic metres, or 860 litres, which is around seventeen 50-litre bags. For more than one bed, a bulk delivery of soil sold by the cubic metre usually costs far less than bags.

Filling a new bed entirely with compost or bagged potting mix is tempting because both are clean, light, and rich, but soil life eats organic matter every year (Lesson 4). A bed of pure compost loses a quarter or more of its height in its first year and keeps shrinking after that. A good general fill is about two parts screened topsoil to one part compost by volume. The mineral grains of the topsoil keep the bed at its height and hold nutrients on their clay, while the compost supplies organic matter and soil life.

Some gardeners fill the bottom of a deep bed with logs and branches to save on soil, a method called **hugelkultur**. Buried wood soaks up water as it rots and feeds fungi for years, but it rots slowly and unevenly, so the soil above keeps falling into the gaps between the logs and the bed keeps sinking. While the wood is fresh, the microbes digesting it also draw nitrogen from the soil above, just as dug-in sawdust does. The figure below compares how far a 30 cm bed sinks with different fills.[^settling]

blocks.task: Find a fill that sinks less than 5 cm in its first year

blocks.text: Whatever the mix, loose fill settles by roughly a tenth in its first season as rain and the weight of the soil collapse its air pockets. Fill the bed in layers 10 to 15 cm deep and water each layer well before adding the next, then mound the final layer a few centimetres above the rim to allow for the settling that remains. Bought topsoil varies widely, so ask the supplier whether it has been screened to remove stones and roots, look through it for the roots of perennial weeds such as couch grass and bindweed, and ask whether it contains manure from fields sprayed with persistent weedkiller (Lesson 4).

parts.title: Joining the bed to the ground

blocks.text: The ground under a raised bed matters as much as its fill, because water and roots have to cross the boundary between them. Water soaking down through fine soil slows sharply where it meets a denser layer, such as trodden ground under a new bed, and collects above it in the same way rain pools on a compacted path (Lesson 2). Water also stops where fine soil sits on a much coarser layer such as gravel, because the fine pores hold onto their water by capillary attraction and release it into the wide pores below only once the soil just above the boundary is saturated.[^boundary] Either kind of sharp boundary leaves the bottom of the bed wetter than the soil above it.

Before filling a bed on open ground, loosen the soil underneath with a digging fork, pushing it in to its full depth and rocking it back without turning the soil over (Lesson 6). Mix the first few centimetres of fill into the loosened surface so that the change from fill to ground is gradual. Over grass or weeds, lay flattened cardboard with its tape removed directly on the ground first. The cardboard smothers the plants beneath it and then rots away within a season, letting worms move up into the bed. Leave out any layer of gravel or rubble at the bottom, since a coarse layer under the fill holds water up in the bed instead of draining it.

Over paving, or over ground that may hold lead from old paint, demolished buildings, or busy roads (Lesson 9), lay a sheet of permeable landscape fabric under the bed to keep the fill separate from the soil below, and make the bed at least 30 cm deep and preferably 45 cm. For the frame, naturally rot-resistant timbers such as larch, cedar, and oak last for many years untreated. Avoid old railway sleepers soaked in creosote, and timber treated before about 2004 with chromated copper arsenate, which can leach arsenic into the soil next to the boards.[^timber]

Spread 2 to 5 cm of compost over a raised bed each year, as you would on any bed (Lesson 4). The compost replaces the organic matter that soil life has eaten and brings the surface back up toward the rim. Turning the bed with a spade or tiller each spring breaks down its crumb and speeds up the sinking, so loosen only where needed and leave the rest of the work to roots and worms.

A raised bed loses water through its sides as well as its surface, and a narrow, tall bed or one with sides of dark metal that heat up in the sun dries out fastest of all. In the first year the loose fill drains especially quickly. Check moisture by pushing a finger 5 cm into the soil a few days after rain or watering, and water deeply when it feels dry, at about 20 to 25 litres per square metre (Lesson 2). A 5 cm mulch of straw, leaf mould, or compost over the surface in summer cuts evaporation sharply.

Because the fill is brought in, its pH and nutrients may differ from the soil in the rest of the garden. Test the pH of a new fill with a kit before the first sowing, and send a sample to a laboratory if plants grow poorly in the first season (Lesson 9).

blocks.title: Try it in the garden
points: Measure how far the surface of each raised bed sits below its rim every spring and write it down. The yearly change shows how fast the fill is settling and how much compost the bed needs to stay level.
Before ordering soil for a new bed, measure its length, width, and depth, work out its volume in litres, and add about a tenth to allow for settling.
A few days after a good rain, push a finger 5 cm into a raised bed and into the open ground beside it to compare how quickly each one dries.

items.question: Why does a raised bed warm up earlier in spring than the ground beside it?
options: Sun and air reach its sides as well as its top
The frame produces heat as it weathers
Compost in the fill is always actively hot
items.why: Soil lifted above the ground has exposed sides that absorb warmth from sun and air. It also drains faster, and drier soil warms more quickly than wet soil.

items.question: How much fill does a bed 2.4 m long, 1.2 m wide, and 30 cm deep need?
options: About 860 litres
About 86 litres
About 8600 litres
items.why: 2.4 times 1.2 times 0.3 is 0.864 cubic metres. Multiplying by 1000 gives about 860 litres, before allowing for settling.

items.question: A raised bed filled with pure compost has sunk by a quarter in its first year. What caused most of the loss?
options: Soil life ate the organic matter, breathing much of it out as carbon dioxide
Rain washed the compost out through the bottom of the bed
The compost slowly turned into sand
items.why: Compost is mostly organic matter, and soil life consumes a share of it every year. Mineral topsoil does not rot, so a mix of about two parts topsoil to one part compost holds its level far better.

items.question: What happens over the years in a raised bed built over a layer of logs and branches?
options: The wood rots slowly, so the soil above keeps sinking into the gaps between the logs
The bed rises as the wood swells
The logs stay unchanged for decades
items.why: Buried wood breaks down over many years and leaves gaps that the soil above falls into. Fresh wood also ties up nitrogen while microbes digest it.

items.question: Why is a layer of gravel at the bottom of a raised bed on soil a poor idea?
options: Water stays in the fine soil above the gravel until that soil is saturated, so the bottom of the bed stays wet
Gravel adds too many nutrients to the soil
Worms eat the gravel and get sick
items.why: Fine pores hold water by capillary attraction and release it into the wide pores of gravel only once the soil just above them is saturated. The gravel holds water up in the bed instead of draining it.

items.question: What should you do to the ground before filling a new raised bed over grass on a heavy soil?
options: Loosen it with a fork without turning it, then lay cardboard over the grass
Lay plastic sheeting to keep the two soils apart
Leave the ground compacted to give the bed a firm base
items.why: Loosened ground lets water and roots cross from the fill into the soil beneath, and cardboard smothers the grass before rotting away within a season.

items.question: Which material should you avoid for the frame of a raised food bed?
options: Old railway sleepers soaked in creosote
Untreated larch boards
Stone or brick
items.why: Creosote and older chromated copper arsenate treatments can leach harmful chemicals into the soil next to the wood. Rot-resistant untreated timber, stone, and brick are safe choices.

items.question: How do you keep an established raised bed at its height and fertility?
options: Spread 2 to 5 cm of compost on top each year
Replace all the soil every spring
Dig it over deeply every autumn
items.why: A yearly layer of compost replaces the organic matter soil life has eaten. Digging speeds up the loss of crumb and makes the bed settle faster.

summary: **Raised beds trade summer water for spring warmth.** They drain faster, warm earlier and stay free of footsteps, but dry out sooner and cost money to fill.
**Choose height for the ground and the gardener.** 20 to 30 cm suits most vegetables over loosened soil; 45 cm or more suits paving, wet or contaminated ground, or working seated.
**Fill with soil, not just compost.** About two parts topsoil to one part compost holds its level; pure compost or buried logs keep sinking.
**Join the bed to the ground below.** Loosen the soil underneath and leave out gravel so water and roots pass straight through.
**Keep it topped up, mulched and deeply watered.** Add 2 to 5 cm of compost a year, and water when it is dry 5 cm down.
**Measure to plan.** Work out the volume before ordering fill, and track how far the surface sinks each year.

warming.title: Wet soil and spring warmth
warming.text: Water takes about five times as much heat as the same weight of rock minerals to warm by one degree, so a waterlogged soil needs far more of the spring sun's energy to warm up than a drained one. Wet soil also loses heat as water evaporates from its surface. A bed that drains quickly after winter rain therefore warms faster, and seeds such as beans and squash that rot in cold, wet soil can go in sooner.

settling.title: Settling rates in the figure
settling.text: The figure assumes that all loose fill settles by about a tenth in its first season, after which topsoil changes little because its minerals do not rot. Compost loses roughly a sixth of its remaining volume each year as soil life consumes it, and buried logs lose about a quarter of their remaining volume each year as they rot and the soil above falls into the gaps. These rates are rough figures drawn from extension advice and gardeners' measurements. Real beds vary with climate, the age of the compost, and how firmly the fill was packed, so any particular bed may sink faster or slower than the figure shows.

boundary.title: Water at a boundary between soils
boundary.text: Water in a fine soil is held in narrow pores by capillary attraction (Lesson 2), which pulls more strongly in narrow pores than in wide ones. When that water reaches a layer of much wider pores, such as gravel or coarse sand, the wide pores cannot pull it out of the narrow ones, and it stays in the fine soil until the soil just above the boundary is saturated and water starts to drip across. Soil scientists call this a **capillary barrier**. Engineers use the same effect on purpose to keep rainwater out of buried waste, and it explains why a gravel layer at the bottom of a pot or a bed keeps the soil above it wet.

timber.title: Treated timber and arsenic
timber.text: Chromated copper arsenate (CCA) protected outdoor timber for decades by soaking it with copper, chromium, and arsenic. Studies found that small amounts of arsenic leached into the soil within a few centimetres of the boards. The United States ended its use for most household timber at the end of 2003, and the European Union restricted it soon after. Most timber treated for garden use today relies on copper compounds without arsenic, and many extension services consider it acceptable for food beds, though some gardeners line the inside of the boards with heavy plastic sheeting to keep soil away from the wood.
